title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
formal:
Does there exist one deterministic primal-simplex algorithm and fixed positive integers \(C,d\) such that the following holds for every promised rational input \((A,b,c,B_0)\)? The linear program is
\[\max\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ x\in\mathbb R^n,\ x\ge0\},\]
where \(A\in\mathbb Q^{m\times n}\) has full row rank, \(1\le m\le n\), the maximum is finite, and \(B_0\) is any supplied feasible basis. Starting at exactly \(B_0\), the algorithm must reach and output a feasible basis \(B_t\) whose nonbasic reduced costs are all nonpositive, using only the legal improving pivots below, in at most \(C(L+1)^d\) total bit operations. Here \(L\) is the binary length of the complete input, including \(B_0\).
definitions:
The input explicitly lists \(m,n\), every entry of \(A,b,c\), and the \(m\) distinct column indices of \(B_0\). Rationals are encoded by signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators; \(L\) includes all entries, signs, dimensions, basis indices and delimiters. The feasible set may be unbounded, but its objective is promised to have a finite maximum. The supplied basis makes it nonempty. There is no nondegeneracy, small-coefficient or conditioning promise. No guarantee is required for inputs violating these promises.

Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A basis \(B\subseteq[n]\) has size \(m\) and invertible submatrix \(A_B\), whose columns are ordered by increasing index. Coordinates of \(x_B\), \(c_B\), and vectors indexed by \(B\) use this same order. Its basic solution \(x(B)\in\mathbb Q^n\) is
\[x(B)_B=A_B^{-1}b,\qquad x(B)_j=0\quad(j\notin B).\]
The basis is feasible exactly when \(x(B)_B\ge0\) coordinatewise. For a nonbasic index \(j\notin B\), its reduced cost is
\[r_j(B)=c_j-c_B^{\mathsf T}A_B^{-1}A_j,\]
where \(A_j\) is column \(j\) of the original matrix.

A legal pivot chooses an entering index \(j\notin B\) with \(r_j(B)>0\). Set \(a=A_B^{-1}A_j\), with coordinates \(a_k\) indexed by \(k\in B\), and set
\[I=\{k\in B:a_k>0\},\qquad
\theta=\min_{k\in I}\frac{x(B)_k}{a_k}.\]
The finite-maximum promise ensures \(I\ne\varnothing\) for such an entering index. Choose any leaving index \(i\in I\) attaining this minimum and replace the current basis by
\[B'=(B\setminus\{i\})\cup\{j\}.\]
This is one pivot. Ties in the ratio test are decided by the algorithm. The new basic solution has coordinate \(\theta\) at \(j\), coordinates \(x(B)_k-\theta a_k\) at the old basic indices, and zero at the other nonbasic indices. If \(\theta=0\), the pivot is degenerate: it changes the basis while keeping the represented point and objective value unchanged. Such pivots are permitted and count in full. A positive step increases the objective by \(\theta r_j(B)\). An exchange with zero or negative entering reduced cost is not a legal pivot here.

The computation is one finite deterministic multitape Turing-machine program over fixed finite tape alphabets. Every tape transition counts toward the bit-time bound. There is no advice, oracle or randomization. All arithmetic is exact; arithmetic on long integers or fractions, basis updates, comparisons, preprocessing, helper computations, memory access and output are charged at their bit cost. The program may inspect the entire numerical input and keep any history that fits within its total time bound. In particular, it is not restricted to a local or memoryless choice rule or to ordinal rankings of the entering variables.

At designated pivot events the program maintains a current feasible basis, initially exactly \(B_0\). Its entire sequence \(B_0,B_1,\ldots,B_t\) must follow the exchanges just defined on the supplied \(A,b,c\). Other computations cannot reset this current basis, skip intermediate pivots, alter the objective or constraints, or substitute an extended formulation. The rule may perform charged computations about other bases or auxiliary problems, but they do not themselves move the current basis. The terminal condition is
\[r_j(B_t)\le0\quad\text{for every }j\in[n]\setminus B_t.\]
Together with feasibility this certifies that \(x(B_t)\) is an exact maximizer. Reaching a vertex with optimal objective value is not a substitute for this basis condition. If \(B_0\) already satisfies it, zero pivots are allowed; when \(m=n\), the condition is vacuous. The question concerns optimization from a supplied feasible basis, not phase-I construction of that basis. One program and one pair of constants must serve all inputs and all permitted starting bases.
answer_criterion:
Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of such a program, or of its logical negation. A positive proof must verify legality of every basis exchange, feasibility throughout, exact terminal reduced costs and a single worst-case polynomial bound on the complete bit computation, including pivot selection and degenerate steps, for every promised input and initial basis.

A negative proof must rule out every finite deterministic program and every fixed polynomial bound in this model. It may establish unavoidable long paths or unavoidable computation needed to choose pivots, but a lower bound restricted to particular rankings, memory restrictions, one pivot rule, or a nonlinear objective does not establish that universal negation. Merely proving that some short path exists without an efficient uniform algorithm is insufficient for a positive answer. Expected or smoothed time, approximate optimality, and a polynomial number of pivots with unbounded selection cost also do not meet the target. No numerical approximation tolerance applies to this yes/no statement.
why: Simplex is a central optimization method whose practical effectiveness has long exceeded its general worst-case guarantees. The question isolates whether exact polynomial-time linear optimization is compatible with its required improving basis exchanges, including degeneracy, and with efficiently choosing every exchange.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

progress.text: Spielman–Teng establish polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex method, with an expectation over perturbed input and dependence on perturbation scale.
The hypercube lower bound applies to the active-set method with nonlinear polynomial objectives.
The convex-quadratic-maximization lower bound strengthens the nonlinear result; it still does not cover linear objectives.
The published degeneracy result limits a block of stalling at a nonoptimal vertex under its improving-direction condition.
Black–Steiner version 2 establishes NP-hardness of shortest monotone pivot sequences, a different requirement from a polynomial-time sequence.
The full ranking-based version 2 retains the unrestricted open question and the stated information, symmetry and memory restrictions of its lower bounds.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The inspected current ranking-based preprint (v2, 10 August 2026) still poses the general pivot-rule question as open. Its lower bounds restrict information and memory; the March stalling theorem is local, the April shortest-path result concerns minimum-length sequences, and the active-set lower bounds have nonlinear objectives. No verified resolution of the exact supplied-feasible-basis deterministic polynomial bit-time target was established in bounded searches. The card remains source_open; this does not claim an exhaustive proof audit.

context_blocks.text: General linear programming has polynomial-time algorithms measured in the binary input size. This card imposes the additional requirement that the computation reach its answer through legal simplex pivots on the given program from the supplied basis. The August 2026 full version of the ranking-based paper still poses the unrestricted pivot-rule question as open.

A short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short improving path to an optimum. A polynomial bit-time rule would bound both the number of its basis exchanges and the work required to choose them. Its bound may depend on coefficient bit lengths; it would not by itself establish a strongly polynomial LP algorithm or a polytope diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy allows many bases to represent one point. Kukharenko and Sanità bound consecutive degenerate improving pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n-m-1\), with efficient implementation when an improving feasible direction is available. Their result controls a block of stalling at that vertex; it does not give a dimension-independent or polynomial-in-input bound on the total number of distinct vertices visited by an arbitrary simplex run.

Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a two-phase shadow-vertex simplex method. The expectation is over Gaussian perturbations around an arbitrary input, with polynomial dependence on dimensions and on \(1/\sigma\), where \(\sigma>0\) is the relative perturbation scale. This does not bound the deterministic worst-case bit time on every unperturbed rational input.

The ranking-based results restrict the information a rule may use. One theorem gives a superpolynomial iteration lower bound in \(n\) for index-ranking rules with \(o(n/\log n)\) memory states. The other gives \(\Omega(2^{\sqrt K})\) iterations for the stated memoryless class based only on rankings by index, reduced cost and objective increase, where \(K\) counts nonzero constraint-matrix entries. The definitions also require choices to respect ranking-preserving relabelings. Memory states are not bits of memory, and \(K\) is not this card's binary input length \(L\). These restricted-information theorems do not exclude algorithms with full numerical access and general polynomial-time history.

Disser and Mosis obtain an all-pivot-rules lower bound for the active-set method with higher-degree polynomial objectives on a hypercube. Bach, Disser, Huiberts and Mosis strengthen this to convex quadratic maximization. The objective is nonlinear and the optimization direction is maximization; neither theorem is an all-rules lower bound for the linear objective required here.

Black and Steiner’s April 2026 revision proves that finding a shortest monotone pivot sequence is NP-hard, already for simple polytopes where vertices are nondegenerate. Thus a polynomial-time algorithm for always finding a shortest sequence would imply P = NP. This card asks for some polynomial-time legal run and does not require its number of pivots to be minimum, so shortest-path hardness alone does not answer it negatively.

category_assignment.reason: The polynomial-time simplex pivot-rule question is worst-case optimization on every rational LP. Preserve its approved Optimization and numerics placement; a smoothed-analysis reference in the detailed review is context, not the question being asked.

sentences: Primal simplex maximizes a rational linear objective by exchanging one entering and one leaving basis column at a time.
The question asks for one deterministic rule that reaches an optimality-certifying basis from every supplied feasible basis in polynomial total bit time.
Each pivot must have positive entering reduced cost and follow the exact minimum-ratio test, with tied and zero-length degenerate pivots included.
The rule may inspect all numerical data and use history, but every computation and basis exchange must fit the same polynomial input-length bound.
Smoothed guarantees, local antistalling results, restricted-information lower bounds and hardness of shortest pivot paths do not settle this unrestricted rule-existence target.

source_formulation.text: The retained target is the deterministic polynomial bit-time question for primal simplex from a supplied feasible basis. The standard equality form, full row rank, initial basis and positive reduced-cost pivots match Section 2 of the ranking-based work; the explicit ratio test and degeneracy convention also match Section 2.1 of Kukharenko–Sanità, with signs reversed from minimization to maximization. The card fixes a finite uniform algorithm and total bit costs. It does not silently strengthen polynomial bit time to a dimension-only strongly polynomial bound or require a shortest pivot sequence.
